# Monetization Redesign: From "Gate the Product" to "Price the Segments"

## 0. Stated assumptions (adjust to your actuals)

| Assumption | Value used |
|---|---|
| MAU | ~5M |
| Paid conversion | 1.8% (~90k subs) |
| Blended net ARPU | ~$0.11–0.13 / MAU / month |
| Current revenue | ~$6–8M ARR |
| Runway pressure | Need credible 3–4× ARPU trajectory visible within 2 quarters, delivered in 4–6 |
| Store rating | Recovered but fragile; ads incident is in review history |

Numbers below are illustrative and structured so you can substitute your own. What matters is the **architecture and the decision rules**.

---

## 1. Diagnosis: why the previous attempts failed

The two failed tests weren't "monetization doesn't work here." They were two specific, avoidable errors:

**Error 1 — Retroactive gating triggered loss aversion.** Aggressive paywalls took away capability users already had. Endowed value is worth ~2–3× unowned value psychologically. Removing it produces uninstalls *and* one-star reviews, and the damage is concentrated in your most engaged users — the exact cohort with the highest willingness to pay. You taxed your best asset.

**Error 2 — Ads were priced in UX, not in dollars.** Intrusive formats (interstitials in the core loop, high-frequency placements) were applied uniformly, including to high-intent and high-value users. Rating damage from ads is *nonlinear and lagging*: store conversion rate falls, organic installs fall, CAC rises — a compounding hit that dwarfs the ad revenue gained.

**The structural error underneath both:** a single monetization mechanism was applied to a heterogeneous population. If 5 segments derive wildly different value, one paywall at one price on one feature set will convert ~2% by construction. Your <2% conversion is not a demand problem; it's a **packaging and price-discrimination problem**.

**Design principles that follow:**

1. **Additive-only gating.** New premium value is built forward; existing free rights are grandfathered permanently and publicly. This alone removes the primary uninstall driver.
2. **Multiple mechanisms, matched to segment psychology.** Subscriptions for habitual high-intent users; consumption pricing for episodic users; ads and commerce for users who will *never* pay cash; partnerships for users whose value to you is distribution, not revenue.
3. **Ads as value exchange, not tax.** Rewarded and opt-in formats in low-intent surfaces only. Ad-free becomes a *feature of the paid tier* — ads then pull subscription conversion instead of fighting it.
4. **Monetize breadth before depth.** Getting 20% of users to pay $1–3 occasionally is safer and larger than getting 3% to pay $15.
5. **Power tests for retention, not for revenue.** Revenue effects are large and fast; retention effects are small and slow. Test design must be built around the small, slow signal (see §5).

---

## 2. Segment model

Run this off behavior, not demographics. Cluster on: session frequency, depth of core action, breadth of feature use, tenure, social graph density, monetization-adjacent signals (exports, storage, collaboration, commerce intent), and any evidence of work/income use. Then build a **supervised propensity model** on top so every user has a live score for (a) pay-propensity, (b) ad-tolerance, (c) churn-fragility.

Representative segmentation (substitute your cluster names):

| # | Segment | ~% of MAU | Value they get | Willingness-to-pay shape | Fragility |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Professionals / income-generating** — product is in their workflow or earns them money | 2–4% | High, continuous, economic | High, price-inelastic; want capability + reliability + support | Low (switching cost high) — but very vocal |
| 2 | **Power enthusiasts** — daily, deep, identity-linked, no money at stake | 5–8% | High, continuous, emotional | Moderate; pay for convenience, status, personalization, ad-free | **Highest** — these are your reviewers and evangelists |
| 3 | **Habitual casual** — near-daily but shallow, single-feature | 35–45% | Moderate, routine | Low for subscription, real for micro-unlocks and ad-free | Medium |
| 4 | **Episodic / event-driven** — dormant then intense bursts (trip, deadline, season, life event) | 20–30% | Very high *during spikes* | Zero for monthly subs, high for on-demand access | Low |
| 5 | **Social / invited** — present because their group is | 10–15% | Derived from others | Zero individually; positive as part of a group plan | Medium |
| 6 | **Lurkers / dormant** | 10–20% | Low | ~Zero cash | Low (already gone in spirit) |
| 7 | **Latent teams / small business** pockets inside 1 & 3 | 0.5–2% | Very high, multi-seat | Highest ARPU in the file, expenses it | Low |

The strategic insight: **segments 4, 5, 6 are ~50% of your base and are structurally unsubscribable.** Every past paywall test asked them to subscribe, they refused, and the aggregate conversion number stayed under 2%. They need entirely different instruments.

---

## 3. The monetization architecture

### 3.1 Subscription: three tiers with real fences

Replace the single paid tier. Choose a **value metric** that (a) scales with value received, (b) is predictable to the user, and (c) users can grow into. Common good choices: items/projects/collaborators, exports/renders, storage, AI-assist actions, history depth.

| Tier | Price (US; PPP-adjusted elsewhere) | Fences / what it buys | Target segment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Free** | $0 | Everything users have today, permanently. Ad-supported (light, see §3.3). Metered access to *new* premium surfaces. | 3, 4, 5, 6 |
| **Plus** | $4.99/mo, $34.99/yr (~42% off) | Ad-free, convenience & speed, personalization/cosmetics, higher capacity on the value metric, unlimited history, no waits | 2, 3 |
| **Pro** | $12.99–14.99/mo, $99/yr | Professional output (high-res/watermark-free/bulk export, API/integrations), priority processing & support, advanced analytics, offline, commercial-use license | 1, 2 (top) |
| **Family / Group** | $9.99/mo up to 5–6 members | Plus features for a household or friend group; shared library/collaboration | 5, plus 2/3 who invite |
| **Teams** | $8–12/seat/mo, 3-seat min | Shared workspace, admin, SSO (later), billing consolidation, seat-based | 7 |

Why three consumer tiers and not two: with one tier you cannot separate "I want ads gone and a bit more room" ($5) from "this is my job" ($15). Adding Pro typically lifts revenue-per-subscriber 20–40% via self-selection with negligible added churn, because Pro buyers were previously *under-charged*, not absent.

Why annual is aggressive: annual plans convert monthly churn risk into a one-time decision, improve cash position (which is the actual investor problem), and raise realized LTV 1.5–2× on the same nominal conversion rate. Push annual as the default-highlighted option with a monthly escape hatch.

**Mechanics that matter more than the price points:**

- **Reverse trial.** New users get 7–14 days of Plus/Pro automatically, then downgrade to Free with their pre-trial rights fully intact. This manufactures the loss-aversion effect *ethically* — they lose something they were given, never something they had earned. Typically the single highest-ROI change available, and it's uninstall-neutral because Free is never worse than before.
- **Metered soft paywall on new premium surfaces only.** e.g., 3 free AI-assists or 2 free advanced exports per month, then upsell. Never metered on the legacy core loop.
- **Contextual, moment-of-value paywalls.** Trigger at the point of demonstrated intent (user hit the capacity ceiling, tried to export, invited a 4th collaborator) — not on launch, not on day 1, not after a crash or a failed action.
- **Permanent grandfathering pledge, published.** "Anything free today stays free for you, forever." Post it, put it in-app, put it in the release notes. This is a rating-protection instrument as much as a policy.
- **PPP/regional pricing.** If a large share of MAU is in low-ARPU markets, local pricing at 25–50% of US typically produces 2–4× local conversion at higher local revenue. Frequently the biggest single unlock for a "millions of free users, low conversion" profile.
- **Segment-aware discounting, not blanket discounting.** Win-back and price-drop offers targeted by pay-propensity score to users who saw a paywall and bounced — never surfaced to users about to convert at full price.
- **Student / creator / non-profit tiers** to capture segment 2 without cannibalizing 1.

### 3.2 Usage-based / consumption pricing (the missing instrument)

This is how you monetize segment 4 (20–30% of MAU), who will never accept a recurring charge but have high, spiky value.

- **Day / week / event passes** — $1.99 day, $4.99 week: full Plus (or Pro) for the burst. Trip, deadline, tournament, tax season, wedding.
- **Credit / token packs** — for metered premium actions (AI generations, exports, boosts, priority processing): $2.99 / $7.99 / $19.99 with volume discounting. Credits price the *cost-bearing* features honestly and let heavy users self-serve past tier ceilings.
- **Overage on subscription tiers** — Plus/Pro include a monthly credit allowance; heavy users buy top-ups. This is how you capture the top 1% without a $50 tier.
- **One-time permanent unlocks** — cosmetics, themes, a specific tool, "remove ads forever" ($14.99–24.99). Segment 3 buys these; the anti-subscription cohort will pay once what they won't pay monthly.
- **Consumption → subscription ladder.** After the 2nd–3rd pass or pack purchase, show the arithmetic: "You've spent $9 in passes; Plus is $4.99/mo." Passes become a paid trial you get paid for.

Expected reach: 10–20% of MAU touch a consumption purchase annually at $2–8 average; a meaningful share ladder into subscription. Critically, **consumption pricing has near-zero churn risk** — nothing is taken away, and the user initiates.

### 3.3 Advertising: rebuilt as value exchange

You cannot afford another ratings incident, but you also cannot leave ~50% of MAU monetized at $0. Ads return under strict constraints:

**Allowed formats**
- **Rewarded video / rewarded interstitial (opt-in).** User chooses to watch to earn credits, unlock a premium action once, extend a pass, or skip a wait. This is the anchor format: opt-in, so it does not degrade the experience of anyone who declines, and it *demonstrates* premium value, lifting subscription conversion.
- **Native placements in low-intent surfaces only** — discovery/browse feeds, end-of-session screens, search results, non-core tabs. Never in the core creation/consumption loop.
- **Brand sponsorships / branded content** — sold direct, curated, higher CPM, no SDK bloat: sponsored challenges, seasonal collections, co-branded templates. Best-of-breed for rating safety because the creative is reviewed by you.
- **Offerwall** for segments 3/6 who want free credits.

**Forbidden (hard product rules)**
- No full-screen interstitials on app open, or interrupting an in-progress core action, or after an error/crash.
- No ads for the first N sessions (let habit form) or for users under 7 days of tenure.
- No ads to users with high pay-propensity while an offer is live (they're worth more converted).
- No ads at all to segment 1 and top-decile segment 2 during the ramp — the reviewer cohort.
- No SDKs that can serve unvetted creative; enforce category blocklists, no autoplay-with-sound, latency budgets, and creative review.

**Load governance**
- Frequency caps: start at **1 non-rewarded impression per 3 sessions**, hard daily cap, minimum time-to-first-ad ≥ 90 seconds of session time.
- Ramp load only when guardrails hold for 14 consecutive days (see §5.5).
- Ad-free is a headline Plus benefit → ads become a conversion driver, not just an ARPU line. Measure this cross-elasticity explicitly.

Realistic yield: with disciplined load, **$0.15–0.35 per free MAU per month** in strong markets, $0.02–0.08 in low-CPM markets. On 4.5M free users, that's ~$0.5–1.2M/month — comparable to your entire current revenue — obtained without touching the core loop.

### 3.4 Partnerships, commerce, and platform revenue

This is where you monetize users who will *never* pay you and shouldn't see ads. Highest margin, lowest UX risk, most underweighted in consumer apps.

# Critique

## A. Showstopper: the deliverable is incomplete, and the missing parts are the ones the request emphasized

The output terminates mid-table in §3.4 (`| Play | M`). That means:

- **§4 (mapping offers to segments) is absent.** §2 gives a segment table and §3 gives an instrument catalog, but the explicit cross-map — for each segment, the primary offer, the trigger, the surface, the expected take rate, and the *excluded* treatments — never appears. Readers must infer it from scattered "target segment" column entries.
- **§5 (experiment plan and guardrail metrics) is absent.** This is roughly half the original ask ("define the experiment plan and guardrail metrics that will catch churn damage before it compounds"), and it is the half the client most needs, given two prior monetization failures. The document forward-references it four times ("see §5", "§5.5", "Measure this cross-elasticity explicitly") and never delivers. Every prescribed ramp rule ("ramp load only when guardrails hold for 14 consecutive days") is therefore inoperable as written.
- **No financial model.** The assumptions table asserts the requirement — "credible 3–4× ARPU trajectory" — but nothing builds up incremental ARPU by segment × instrument to show whether the architecture actually clears that bar. An investor-facing strategy that does not close its own loop on the stated financial target is not decision-ready.
- **No sequencing/roadmap.** Given a 2-quarter visibility constraint, the omission of what ships in weeks 0–4 vs. Q1 vs. Q2 is material. Several proposed instruments (direct-sold brand sponsorships, SSO, Teams billing) have 2–3 quarter lead times and cannot contribute inside the runway window; the document doesn't flag this.

## B. Analytical errors and internal inconsistencies in the delivered portion

1. **Segment table doesn't reconcile.** Midpoints sum to ~103%; upper bounds sum to ~132%; segment 7 is explicitly a subset of 1 and 3. Fine as a sketch, but it's presented as a quantified base for the claim that "segments 4, 5, 6 are ~50% of your base" — a load-bearing number that ranges from 40% to 65% depending on which end you read. Either make the segmentation MECE with shares summing to 100% and overlaps handled as tags, or stop deriving quantities from it.

2. **The ad yield estimate contradicts the ad load governance.** §3.3 prescribes ≤1 non-rewarded impression per 3 sessions, no ads before day 7, no ads to segment 1 or top-decile segment 2, and no ads to high-pay-propensity users with a live offer — then projects $0.15–0.35 per free MAU/month. # Monetization Redesign: From "Gate the Product" to "Price the Segments"

## 0. Stated assumptions (adjust to your actuals)

| Assumption | Value used |
|---|---|
| MAU | ~5M |
| Paid conversion | 1.8% (~90k subs) |
| Blended net ARPU | ~$0.11–0.13 / MAU / month |
| Current revenue | ~$6–8M ARR |
| Runway pressure | Need credible 3–4× ARPU trajectory visible within 2 quarters, delivered in 4–6 |
| Store rating | Recovered but fragile; ads incident is in review history |

Numbers below are illustrative and structured so you can substitute your own. What matters is the **architecture and the decision rules**.

---

## 1. Diagnosis: why the previous attempts failed

The two failed tests weren't "monetization doesn't work here." They were two specific, avoidable errors:

**Error 1 — Retroactive gating triggered loss aversion.** Aggressive paywalls took away capability users already had. Endowed value is worth ~2–3× unowned value psychologically. Removing it produces uninstalls *and* one-star reviews, and the damage is concentrated in your most engaged users — the exact cohort with the highest willingness to pay. You taxed your best asset.

**Error 2 — Ads were priced in UX, not in dollars.** Intrusive formats (interstitials in the core loop, high-frequency placements) were applied uniformly, including to high-intent and high-value users. Rating damage from ads is *nonlinear and lagging*: store conversion rate falls, organic installs fall, CAC rises — a compounding hit that dwarfs the ad revenue gained.

**The structural error underneath both:** a single monetization mechanism was applied to a heterogeneous population. If 5 segments derive wildly different value, one paywall at one price on one feature set will convert ~2% by construction. Your <2% conversion is not a demand problem; it's a **packaging and price-discrimination problem**.

**Design principles that follow:**

1. **Additive-only gating.** New premium value is built forward; existing free rights are grandfathered permanently and publicly. This alone removes the primary uninstall driver.
2. **Multiple mechanisms, matched to segment psychology.** Subscriptions for habitual high-intent users; consumption pricing for episodic users; ads and commerce for users who will *never* pay cash; partnerships for users whose value to you is distribution, not revenue.
3. **Ads as value exchange, not tax.** Rewarded and opt-in formats in low-intent surfaces only. Ad-free becomes a *feature of the paid tier* — ads then pull subscription conversion instead of fighting it.
4. **Monetize breadth before depth.** Getting 20% of users to pay $1–3 occasionally is safer and larger than getting 3% to pay $15.
5. **Power tests for retention, not for revenue.** Revenue effects are large and fast; retention effects are small and slow. Test design must be built around the small, slow signal (see §5).

---

## 2. Segment model

Run this off behavior, not demographics. Cluster on: session frequency, depth of core action, breadth of feature use, tenure, social graph density, monetization-adjacent signals (exports, storage, collaboration, commerce intent), and any evidence of work/income use. Then build a **supervised propensity model** on top so every user has a live score for (a) pay-propensity, (b) ad-tolerance, (c) churn-fragility.

Representative segmentation (substitute your cluster names):

| # | Segment | ~% of MAU | Value they get | Willingness-to-pay shape | Fragility |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Professionals / income-generating** — product is in their workflow or earns them money | 2–4% | High, continuous, economic | High, price-inelastic; want capability + reliability + support | Low (switching cost high) — but very vocal |
| 2 | **Power enthusiasts** — daily, deep, identity-linked, no money at stake | 5–8% | High, continuous, emotional | Moderate; pay for convenience, status, personalization, ad-free | **Highest** — these are your reviewers and evangelists |
| 3 | **Habitual casual** — near-daily but shallow, single-feature | 35–45% | Moderate, routine | Low for subscription, real for micro-unlocks and ad-free | Medium |
| 4 | **Episodic / event-driven** — dormant then intense bursts (trip, deadline, season, life event) | 20–30% | Very high *during spikes* | Zero for monthly subs, high for on-demand access | Low |
| 5 | **Social / invited** — present because their group is | 10–15% | Derived from others | Zero individually; positive as part of a group plan | Medium |
| 6 | **Lurkers / dormant** | 10–20% | Low | ~Zero cash | Low (already gone in spirit) |
| 7 | **Latent teams / small business** pockets inside 1 & 3 | 0.5–2% | Very high, multi-seat | Highest ARPU in the file, expenses it | Low |

The strategic insight: **segments 4, 5, 6 are ~50% of your base and are structurally unsubscribable.** Every past paywall test asked them to subscribe, they refused, and the aggregate conversion number stayed under 2%. They need entirely different instruments.

---

## 3. The monetization architecture

### 3.1 Subscription: three tiers with real fences

Replace the single paid tier. Choose a **value metric** that (a) scales with value received, (b) is predictable to the user, and (c) users can grow into. Common good choices: items/projects/collaborators, exports/renders, storage, AI-assist actions, history depth.

| Tier | Price (US; PPP-adjusted elsewhere) | Fences / what it buys | Target segment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Free** | $0 | Everything users have today, permanently. Ad-supported (light, see §3.3). Metered access to *new* premium surfaces. | 3, 4, 5, 6 |
| **Plus** | $4.99/mo, $34.99/yr (~42% off) | Ad-free, convenience & speed, personalization/cosmetics, higher capacity on the value metric, unlimited history, no waits | 2, 3 |
| **Pro** | $12.99–14.99/mo, $99/yr | Professional output (high-res/watermark-free/bulk export, API/integrations), priority processing & support, advanced analytics, offline, commercial-use license | 1, 2 (top) |
| **Family / Group** | $9.99/mo up to 5–6 members | Plus features for a household or friend group; shared library/collaboration | 5, plus 2/3 who invite |
| **Teams** | $8–12/seat/mo, 3-seat min | Shared workspace, admin, SSO (later), billing consolidation, seat-based | 7 |

Why three consumer tiers and not two: with one tier you cannot separate "I want ads gone and a bit more room" ($5) from "this is my job" ($15). Adding Pro typically lifts revenue-per-subscriber 20–40% via self-selection with negligible added churn, because Pro buyers were previously *under-charged*, not absent.

Why annual is aggressive: annual plans convert monthly churn risk into a one-time decision, improve cash position (which is the actual investor problem), and raise realized LTV 1.5–2× on the same nominal conversion rate. Push annual as the default-highlighted option with a monthly escape hatch.

**Mechanics that matter more than the price points:**

- **Reverse trial.** New users get 7–14 days of Plus/Pro automatically, then downgrade to Free with their pre-trial rights fully intact. This manufactures the loss-aversion effect *ethically* — they lose something they were given, never something they had earned. Typically the single highest-ROI change available, and it's uninstall-neutral because Free is never worse than before.
- **Metered soft paywall on new premium surfaces only.** e.g., 3 free AI-assists or 2 free advanced exports per month, then upsell. Never metered on the legacy core loop.
- **Contextual, moment-of-value paywalls.** Trigger at the point of demonstrated intent (user hit the capacity ceiling, tried to export, invited a 4th collaborator) — not on launch, not on day 1, not after a crash or a failed action.
- **Permanent grandfathering pledge, published.** "Anything free today stays free for you, forever." Post it, put it in-app, put it in the release notes. This is a rating-protection instrument as much as a policy.
- **PPP/regional pricing.** If a large share of MAU is in low-ARPU markets, local pricing at 25–50% of US typically produces 2–4× local conversion at higher local revenue. Frequently the biggest single unlock for a "millions of free users, low conversion" profile.
- **Segment-aware discounting, not blanket discounting.** Win-back and price-drop offers targeted by pay-propensity score to users who saw a paywall and bounced — never surfaced to users about to convert at full price.
- **Student / creator / non-profit tiers** to capture segment 2 without cannibalizing 1.

### 3.2 Usage-based / consumption pricing (the missing instrument)

This is how you monetize segment 4 (20–30% of MAU), who will never accept a recurring charge but have high, spiky value.

- **Day / week / event passes** — $1.99 day, $4.99 week: full Plus (or Pro) for the burst. Trip, deadline, tournament, tax season, wedding.
- **Credit / token packs** — for metered premium actions (AI generations, exports, boosts, priority processing): $2.99 / $7.99 / $19.99 with volume discounting. Credits price the *cost-bearing* features honestly and let heavy users self-serve past tier ceilings.
- **Overage on subscription tiers** — Plus/Pro include a monthly credit allowance; heavy users buy top-ups. This is how you capture the top 1% without a $50 tier.
- **One-time permanent unlocks** — cosmetics, themes, a specific tool, "remove ads forever" ($14.99–24.99). Segment 3 buys these; the anti-subscription cohort will pay once what they won't pay monthly.
- **Consumption → subscription ladder.** After the 2nd–3rd pass or pack purchase, show the arithmetic: "You've spent $9 in passes; Plus is $4.99/mo." Passes become a paid trial you get paid for.

Expected reach: 10–20% of MAU touch a consumption purchase annually at $2–8 average; a meaningful share ladder into subscription. Critically, **consumption pricing has near-zero churn risk** — nothing is taken away, and the user initiates.

### 3.3 Advertising: rebuilt as value exchange

You cannot afford another ratings incident, but you also cannot leave ~50% of MAU monetized at $0. Ads return under strict constraints:

**Allowed formats**
- **Rewarded video / rewarded interstitial (opt-in).** User chooses to watch to earn credits, unlock a premium action once, extend a pass, or skip a wait. This is the anchor format: opt-in, so it does not degrade the experience of anyone who declines, and it *demonstrates* premium value, lifting subscription conversion.
- **Native placements in low-intent surfaces only** — discovery/browse feeds, end-of-session screens, search results, non-core tabs. Never in the core creation/consumption loop.
- **Brand sponsorships / branded content** — sold direct, curated, higher CPM, no SDK bloat: sponsored challenges, seasonal collections, co-branded templates. Best-of-breed for rating safety because the creative is reviewed by you.
- **Offerwall** for segments 3/6 who want free credits.

**Forbidden (hard product rules)**
- No full-screen interstitials on app open, or interrupting an in-progress core action, or after an error/crash.
- No ads for the first N sessions (let habit form) or for users under 7 days of tenure.
- No ads to users with high pay-propensity while an offer is live (they're worth more converted).
- No ads at all to segment 1 and top-decile segment 2 during the ramp — the reviewer cohort.
- No SDKs that can serve unvetted creative; enforce category blocklists, no autoplay-with-sound, latency budgets, and creative review.

**Load governance**
- Frequency caps: start at **1 non-rewarded impression per 3 sessions**, hard daily cap, minimum time-to-first-ad ≥ 90 seconds of session time.
- Ramp load only when guardrails hold for 14 consecutive days (see §5.5).
- Ad-free is a headline Plus benefit → ads become a conversion driver, not just an ARPU line. Measure this cross-elasticity explicitly.

Realistic yield: with disciplined load, **$0.15–0.35 per free MAU per month** in strong markets, $0.02–0.08 in low-CPM markets. On 4.5M free users, that's ~$0.5–1.2M/month — comparable to your entire current revenue — obtained without touching the core loop.

### 3.4 Partnerships, commerce, and platform revenue

This is where you monetize users who will *never* pay you and shouldn't see ads. Highest margin, lowest UX risk, most underweighted in consumer apps.

- **Privacy/regulatory absent:** ATT/consent effects on CPMs, GDPR/TCF consent flows (which themselves reduce fill and can annoy users), COPPA/age gating if minors are present, and legal exposure for behavioral price discrimination in certain jurisdictions. Also no mention of the data-sharing implications of the commerce/partnership plays.
- **VPN/store-region arbitrage** on PPP pricing, and cannibalization risk for mid-tier markets currently paying US prices.
- **No downside case.** There is no "what if ARPU only doubles" or "what if ads again cost more in organic installs than they earn" scenario, and no explicit kill criteria or rollback plan per instrument.

## E. Presentation

- Strong structure and skimmability; the diagnosis section is genuinely good. But the register is *assertive-consultant*, and the ratio of confident benchmarks to labeled uncertainty is too high for a plan whose entire premise is "we already got this wrong twice."
- Forward references to a section that doesn't exist make the document read as a draft, not a deliverable.
- The assumptions table is good practice, but it embeds a *requirement* ("need 3–4× ARPU") as an assumption without ever testing feasibility against the proposed levers.

## F. What genuinely works (keep)

- The reframe from "demand problem" to "packaging and price-discrimination problem" is the correct diagnosis and is argued crisply.
- Additive-only gating + reverse trial as the ethical substitute for retroactive loss aversion is the right core mechanic.
- Naming ~50% of the base as "structurally unsubscribable" and assigning them different instruments (consumption, rewarded, commerce) is the key insight the client's prior tests lacked.
- "Ads as conversion driver via ad-free as a paid benefit" and measuring the cross-elasticity explicitly.
- Principle 5 — "power tests for retention, not for revenue" — is the single most sophisticated line in the document. It's also the one that most needed the missing §5 to be actionable.
- Consumption→subscription ladder framed as "a paid trial you get paid for."
